nameStory: Fountain Apple-moss gets its charming name from its distinctive sporophytes (spore capsules) that arch gracefully outward like water spraying from a fountain. The 'apple' part comes from the round, apple-shaped capsules that dangle at the tips of curved stalks. When a patch is in full sporophyte, it really does look like dozens of tiny green fountains sprouting from the moss carpet!
description: Fountain Apple-moss is a small but distinctive moss that forms loose, bright green cushions or mats in wet areas. Individual plants are tiny, usually only about half an inch tall, but they often grow together in patches several inches across. The most eye-catching feature is the curved sporophytes that arch outward from the plant like miniature shepherd's crooks, each topped with a round, apple-shaped capsule. This is one of the easier mosses to identify when it's producing its characteristic fountain-like sporophytes.

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Curved, arching stalks that bend outward like tiny shepherd's crooks, each topped with a round, green to brown capsule that looks like a miniature apple

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, bright green cushions or low mats, with individual shoots standing upright like tiny soldiers in formation

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves that feel slightly rough to the touch and spiral around the stem, becoming more crowded toward the shoot tips

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright yellow-green when wet and actively growing, becoming duller green to brownish when dry

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found in constantly moist to wet conditions - never in dry spots like many other small mosses

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels soft and spongy when wet, but becomes somewhat crispy and brittle when dried out

habitat: Fountain Apple-moss thrives in constantly wet or boggy areas throughout New England's mountains and wetlands. Look for it along stream banks, in wet meadows, around seeps and springs, and in the soggy edges of ponds and marshes. It particularly loves areas where water slowly trickles over soil or rocks, living up to its fountain-loving nature.

seasonality.spring: Sporophytes begin developing in late spring, appearing as tiny curved stalks. The moss is bright green and actively growing in the abundant moisture.
seasonality.summer: Peak sporophyte season when the distinctive fountain-like capsules are most visible and mature. Plants remain vibrant green in wet conditions.
seasonality.fall: Sporophytes may persist into fall but begin to darken and age. The moss starts to slow its growth as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Most sporophytes have fallen or withered, but the moss remains evergreen under snow. Growth is minimal but plants survive freezing.

funFact: Fountain Apple-moss capsules actually explode to release their spores! When ripe, the round capsules split open with tiny pops that can sometimes be heard on quiet days, shooting microscopic spores up to several inches away - their own miniature fireworks display.
confusionNotes: Without sporophytes, Fountain Apple-moss can look like many other small wet-area mosses, but remember the habitat clue: if it's not in consistently wet conditions, it's probably not Fountain Apple-moss. The curved, fountain-like sporophytes are unmistakable when present.
compareHints: Fountain Apple-moss differs from its relative Philonotis marchica by its preference for wetter habitats and more consistently curved sporophytes. While both have apple-shaped capsules, Fountain Apple-moss sporophytes arch more dramatically outward, creating that distinctive fountain effect. [Note: Some details about P. marchica comparison are uncertain due to limited reference material.]
